title: Linked List Cycle
corePattern: Floyd's Cycle Finding Algorithm (Fast and Slow Pointers)
interviewTips: Clarify cycle definition: ask if cycle means revisiting same node object by reference, not equal values, and how input pos is given.
Trade-off to articulate: Hash Set is intuitive and O(n) space vs Floyd is O(1) space with same O(n) time - interviewers expect Floyd as follow-up.
Edge-case tip: explicitly handle empty list, single node without cycle, and single node self-loop to avoid null pointer errors.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Brute Force with Hash Set
approaches.intuition: If we walk the list and ever visit the same node object twice, there must be a cycle. Remember every visited node in a set and check for repeats.
approaches.theory: Traverse from head following next pointers. Maintain a set of visited node identities (references/pointers). For each curr, if curr is already in set return True, else add it and move to curr.next. If we reach null, no cycle exists. Correct because a cycle causes infinite revisit of same objects, while an acyclic list has n distinct nodes and terminates.

timeComplexity.explanation: Each of n nodes visited at most once with O(1) average hash set insert and lookup.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Stores up to n node references in hash set in worst case of acyclic list.

dryRunExample.input: head = [3,2,0,-4], pos = 1 (tail connects to node index 1 with value 2)
steps: curr=3 not in {} -> add 3, move to 2
curr=2 not in {3} -> add 2, move to 0
curr=0 not in {3,2} -> add 0, move to -4
curr=-4 not in {3,2,0} -> add -4, move to 2 (cycle edge)
curr=2 already in set -> return True

edgeCases: Single node without cycle head=[1], pos=-1 -> returns False
Single node self-loop head=[1], pos=0 -> detects repeat and returns True
Two nodes with cycle [1,2], pos=0 -> returns True

approaches.name: Approach 2: Optimal Floyd Tortoise and Hare
approaches.intuition: Imagine two runners on a track: slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2 steps. On a straight track fast runs away to the end, on a circular track fast laps and meets slow.
approaches.theory: Initialize slow=head and fast=head. While fast and fast.next are not null, advance slow by 1 and fast by 2. If slow==fast, cycle exists. Proof: if no cycle, fast reaches null. If cycle of length C exists, after entering cycle the distance between fast and slow shrinks by 1 each iteration modulo C, so they must meet within C steps. Uses only pointer comparison, no extra storage.

timeComplexity.explanation: Fast pointer traverses at most 2n steps. Acyclic case O(n), cyclic case slow enters cycle after k steps then meets within cycle length, still linear.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only two pointers slow and fast, no extra data structure proportional to input.

steps: slow=3, fast=3, fast and fast.next exist
iter2: slow=0, fast=2 (fast went -4 -> 2 via cycle), not equal
iter3: slow=-4, fast=-4 (fast went 0 -> -4 -> -4? actually 0->-4->2->0->-4), equal -> return True

edgeCases: Empty list head=null -> loop condition fails, returns False
Single node no cycle: fast.next is null -> returns False
Single node self-loop: slow and fast meet after 1 iteration -> returns True
Long tail + small cycle: still meets without null dereference due to fast and fast.next checks
